cards.front: Why do cellulose chains stay straight and unbranched, while starch chains coil or branch?
cards.back: Cellulose uses **beta-glucose**, and every second unit is turned upside down so the bonds line up. This gives straight chains that can lie side by side.
cards.hint: Compare how the two glucose forms join with their neighbours.

cards.front: How do straight cellulose chains give a plant cell wall its strength?
cards.back: Chains lie side by side and many **hydrogen bonds** form between neighbouring chains. Bundled together as microfibrils, they resist pulling forces.
cards.hint: Think about how the chains sit relative to each other.

cards.front: Why is starch well suited to storing glucose?
cards.back: It is compact, so much glucose fits in a small space. It is insoluble, so it does not draw water in by osmosis. Its many branch ends let enzymes release glucose quickly.
cards.hint: Think about size, solubility and where enzymes can act.

cards.back: A **polysaccharide** is a polymer made of many sugar units joined by glycosidic bonds.
cards.hint: Think about what the prefix poly- means.

cards.back: A **glycosidic bond** is the covalent bond formed between two sugar units in a condensation reaction.

cards.front: What is the only difference between alpha-glucose and beta-glucose?
cards.back: The position of the $\text{OH}$ group on carbon 1: it points down in alpha-glucose and up in beta-glucose.
cards.hint: Compare a diagram of the two forms side by side.

cards.front: What happens, step by step, when two glucose units join?
cards.back: 1) Two sugar units come together. 2) A condensation reaction removes a molecule of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. 3) A glycosidic bond forms between them.
cards.hint: Look at which molecule leaves the sugars.

cards.back: An **unbranched** chain of alpha-glucose units joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds, which coils into a helix.
cards.hint: Contrast it with the branched form in starch.

cards.back: A **branched** polymer of alpha-glucose with 1,4 bonds in its chains and 1,6 bonds at the branch points.
cards.hint: Think about which starch component has side branches.

cards.back: An **unbranched** beta-glucose polysaccharide that provides strength in plant cell walls.
**Weak attractions** between a slightly positive hydrogen atom and a slightly negative atom, such as oxygen.
cards.hint: Think about charge on atoms in neighbouring OH groups.

cards.front: Why is cellulose better suited to a permanent wall than starch is to storage?
cards.back: Cellulose is rigid and hard for most enzymes to break down, so it stays in place. Starch is easy to hydrolyse, so its glucose can be released when needed.
cards.hint: Think about how easily each polymer is broken down.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say that one hydrogen bond makes cellulose very strong?
cards.back: Each hydrogen bond is **weak** on its own. Strength comes from thousands of them acting together between neighbouring chains.
**Strong bundles** of cellulose chains held together by hydrogen bonds.
